prize_parts.citation: For the invention of the magic-wavelength optical lattice clock and its realisation at the 10^-18 level of fractional uncertainty

statement.case_for: I keep B004 as a single part for Katori and Ye. Katori's magic-wavelength lattice is a concrete invention: it removes the trap-induced shift so that a large ensemble of neutral atoms can be held in the Lamb-Dicke regime and interrogated on an ultranarrow line. Ye's group then showed that this delivers fractional uncertainty near 1e-18 together with record stability, and that many-body interactions in a degenerate Fermi gas are both a systematic to be controlled and a resource. That is the combination of an original idea and a decisive realisation that our criteria ask for. The result has been reproduced and compared in several laboratories over about two decades, the interpretation is stable, and it is used for tests of fundamental constants, millimetre-scale gravitational redshift and dark-sector searches. Reading the round-1 files, I note that the supporting arguments (originality, attribution, confirmation) are the same across seven members and do not depend on the vote count, which is why I rest my own position on them. I ranked B004 eighth in my opening ballot. I have already said that this reflected my own field's pull and overlap worry, and the round-1 discussion has not given me a scientific reason to go back to that placement.
statement.case_against: The distinctness question is real and I cannot dismiss it as a formality. The 2005 prize covered the frequency comb and precision laser spectroscopy, and the 2012 prize covered control of single trapped quantum systems, and both sit under modern optical clocks. My judgement, which is that of a theorist in superconducting circuits and not a specialist in atomic metrology, is that the lattice clock is a different regime: a single ion is limited in statistics by one absorber, whereas the magic-wavelength lattice trades that limit for many atoms without Doppler, recoil or trap shifts, so it improves stability and accuracy at once. That argument is a judgement, not a proof, and Danielsson's point that a prize for a measurement capability is weighed differently from a discovery in nature remains a fair objection. A second reservation is credit beyond the pair (Takamoto and Sr-lattice colleagues in Katori's group, PTB, NIST, SYRTE, and ion-clock groups). I cannot verify the priority record from the supplied material, so I treat it as an unresolved limitation, not as a defect that changes the names. The redefinition of the second has not happened, but I regard it as supporting evidence only and not as a condition.

responses.point: This is a prize for an instrument and measurement capability more than for a new phenomenon, and Danielsson fears choosing the more comfortable attribution over the more consequential discovery (B032, IceCube).
responses.response: I take that fear seriously and agree that a discovery in nature should be weighed heavily; I do not want us to choose B004 merely because the credit is easy. But the lattice clock is not only an instrument: the many-body physics of a degenerate Fermi gas and the millimetre-scale redshift measurement are results about nature that this device made accessible. I also do not think the IceCube choice becomes safer by waiting; the problem I see is that three names for a collaboration of hundreds is a judgement that you yourself say rests on unverified recollection. I would revisit B032 when the source associations firm up, as you suggest, but this year I do not see an attribution I could defend.

responses.point: The strongest reservation is attribution and breadth, since Takamoto and colleagues in Katori's group and the ion-clock and comb contributions are not covered by the credited pair; Kroll also discloses a research stay in Hall's laboratory at JILA, Ye's institution.
responses.response: On the citation I would build on your concern and on the chair's question: the wording should name the magic-wavelength lattice clock and its realisation at 1e-18, not timekeeping in general, so that it does not claim the whole optical-clock field. On the supplied record I see nothing that supports adding Takamoto or any other name, and a three-name limit would not accommodate the groups at PTB, NIST and SYRTE anyway. As for your stay at JILA, a historical doctoral link with no documented tie to Katori or Ye seems to me adequately handled by the disclosure you made; I do not think it bears on B004, and I would not ask for more unless a collaboration with Ye emerges.

responses.point: Pearce frames B004 as an advance in what can be measured and how well, while noting that Ye built much of his record on comb and cavity-stabilised laser technology that is partly prize-recognised already, and cites my eighth-place ranking as a real concern about novelty.
responses.response: Your reference to my eighth place is fair, and I want to answer it directly: that worry about novelty was the reason for it, and I now think it is answered by the single-atom versus many-atom distinction I set out in my case against. Your point about Ye's reliance on comb and laser stabilisation is the more substantial one. It means the Ye part of the credit should rest on the lattice-clock performance and the many-body work and not on the underlying frequency-comb or laser technology, which is why my citation says invention and realisation of the lattice clock and does not mention the comb or laser stabilisation. I also correct a point from round 1, answering the chair: my statement that Ye is credited under other candidate lines was wrong. The shortlist shows him only under B004, and I withdraw that remark.

responses.point: Lindroth asks whether the redefinition of the second is a condition or only supporting evidence, and judges the novelty objection answered by the magic-wavelength lattice being a distinct concept with a qualitative gain over the earlier generation.
responses.response: I answer your question directly: the redefinition is supporting evidence only. The scientific case rests on the invention and on 1e-18 performance confirmed in other laboratories, and requiring a formal SI decision would make our award depend on the metrology bodies' timetable. I agree with your distinctness argument and as a non-specialist I rest on it, but I would ask you, as the atomic physicist, to say whether a few-order-of-magnitude gain over the earlier optical clocks is really independent of the single-ion approach, because if that is false my own position would weaken. As things stand I find your reasoning more persuasive than the opposite view.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers B010 as a single part, calling the 2011 Bistritzer-MacDonald prediction followed by the 2018 discovery of correlated insulating and superconducting states a rare case of prediction organising a discovery, and names B004 as his first alternative.
responses.response: Your argument is the strongest rival to mine, and I do not dismiss it: a tunable parameter that sets correlation strength in a clean material is a genuine step for condensed matter, and I keep B010 as my first alternative for that reason. I differ on timing and credit. A discovery eight years old with an unsettled pairing mechanism, and with Lopes dos Santos, Peres and Castro Neto, the first author of the 2018 papers and several parallel groups outside the three names, is the kind of three-person allocation that I could not defend as exact today. Your own case-against says B004 would be the safer choice, and I think that safer choice is also scientifically sound, not just safe. I would welcome your answer on what you would need to see on the credit question before you would accept B004.

uncertainties: Whether the lattice clock is judged a regime distinct from the 2005 and 2012 prizes; I rely on a theorist's reading of the single-ion versus many-atom distinction and defer to the atomic physicists on it.
Whether Takamoto and other Sr and Yb lattice contributors, or the groups at PTB, NIST and SYRTE, should change the credit; I cannot verify the priority record from the supplied material.
Whether the committee accepts that the redefinition of the second is supporting evidence only; I hold that it is.
Whether B010 will be ready in a few years, once the pairing mechanism and the allocation among MacDonald, Bistritzer, Jarillo-Herrero and others are clearer.
statement.conflict_note: Updated disclosure. I ranked circuit QED (B034) first in my opening ballot and work in the same area: I am at Chalmers and direct WACQT, with Chalmers colleagues Per Delsing and C. M. Wilson and my frequent co-author Anton Frisk Kockum as documented connections, and Chalmers hosted researchers associated with the 2025 prize. I would recuse myself from the decisive discussion of B034 if it became a serious contender, and I have therefore not listed it among my alternatives. I note Olsson's shared Chalmers affiliation and see no issue for B004 from it. No specific conflict with B004, B010 or B023 is apparent from the provided profile. I correct my round-1 remark that Ye appears under other candidate lines: the shortlist shows him only under B004.
